title: Modi Meets Trump Wednesday at G7. Trade, Visas, and Three Dead Sailors Are All on the Table.
excerpt: The bilateral comes as Washington threatens a 12.5 per cent tariff, H-1B approvals have dropped 40 per cent, and India has twice summoned the U.S. envoy over the killing of Indian sailors in the Gulf.
body:
Narendra Modi will sit down with Donald Trump on Wednesday at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France — a bilateral meeting loaded with more friction than either side would prefer to acknowledge.

The White House confirmed the schedule on Saturday: Trump arrives Monday afternoon, holds a leaders' dinner with Emmanuel Macron, then spends Tuesday meeting the Emir of Qatar, the Egyptian president, and the UAE's Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed. Modi gets his slot on Wednesday. No meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy is on the books — the Ukraine war has been, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio admitted last month, effectively on pause while Washington focuses on Iran.

## Trade, Visas, and a $12.5 Billion Ultimatum

The agenda is dense. An Indian government source told Reuters that trade ties, energy cooperation, and H-1B visas would all be on the table. The trade picture is particularly urgent: Washington has proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from India and several other countries, citing allegations of forced labour that India has firmly rejected.


![Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg)


Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said last week that the first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement could be concluded by mid-July. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will travel to India the week after the G7 summit to continue negotiations, a senior U.S. official confirmed. India is pushing for preferential tariff treatment, while the U.S. wants concessions on market access and agricultural imports.



> **"The foreign ministry called the use of lethal force against civilian shipping "unacceptable." Opposition leaders have demanded that Modi raise the issue directly with Trump."**


For the 4.5 million-strong Indian diaspora in America, the visa conversation matters most. A federal judge struck down Trump's $100,000 H-1B fee last week, calling it an unconstitutional tax — but the administration has signaled it will appeal. Indian IT firms saw 40 per cent fewer H-1B approvals this year, with TCS hit hardest. The State Department has also rolled out a $750 fast-track fee for visa interviews, adding yet another financial barrier.

## Three Dead Sailors in the Room


![Donald Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)


The meeting comes days after India summoned the American chargé d'affaires twice over the killing of three Indian sailors in a U.S. naval strike on a tanker off Oman. The foreign ministry called the use of lethal force against civilian shipping "unacceptable." Opposition leaders have demanded that Modi raise the issue directly with Trump.

The U.S.-Iran peace deal, announced just hours ago, may defuse some of that anger. But the families of the dead sailors — and the Indian merchant marine community, which employs roughly 240,000 people — will be watching to see whether Modi extracts more than a diplomatic expression of regret.

## Energy: Oil and Nuclear

With the Strait of Hormuz reopening, energy cooperation moves from crisis management to strategic planning. India and the U.S. signed a ten-year defence framework last week, covering everything from Javelin anti-tank missiles to jet engines. Nuclear energy cooperation, revived under the 2008 civil nuclear deal, is also expected to feature — India recently waived customs duties on nuclear equipment going back seven years, a signal that it is serious about scaling up its nuclear capacity.


![The White House — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg/3840px-White_House_north_and_south_sides.jpg)


The broader backdrop is a relationship under unusual stress. Trump has repeatedly claimed — and India has repeatedly denied — that he intervened to end India's brief conflict with Pakistan last year. The tariff threat, the visa squeeze, and the sailor deaths have created a moment where both sides need a reset more than either wants to admit.

## What NRIs Should Watch For

The Modi-Trump meeting will be closely parsed by the diaspora for three signals: whether the 12.5 per cent tariff threat is walked back, whether there is any movement on H-1B visa caps or processing times, and whether Trump acknowledges the sailor killings in a way that goes beyond boilerplate.

Goyal's mid-July deadline for a trade deal gives the meeting a concrete timeline. If Greer's India visit the following week produces a framework, the tariff threat could recede. If it doesn't, Indian exporters — and the NRIs whose families depend on that export economy — will feel the squeeze well before the American midterm debate heats up.

Modi's European tour, which began in Nice on Friday and included a historic stop in Slovakia — the first by an Indian prime minister since the country's independence in 1993 — has been about projecting India as a serious, multilateral partner. The Wednesday meeting with Trump will test whether that projection translates into concessions on the issues that matter most to ordinary Indians at home and abroad.
